#9724. Decision Models in Hugging Face

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits ($z_1,\ldots,z_K$), (with K classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:

pi=exp⁡(zi/T)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i/T)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​/T)​

∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

The model again produces a probability distribution:

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable (X) representing the level, the expectation is:

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7

This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p)

P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with (K) options, the confidence is:

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​

where ($p_{\max}$) is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.80:

C=3(0.99)−12=0.98 C=\frac{3(0.99)-1}{2}=0.98 C=23(0.99)−1​=0.98

Notice that the winning probability is 0.99, but the reported confidence is 0.98. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:

We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:

First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

Great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that says whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator

For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

#9722. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

In this article, we have taken a look at some of the biggest benefits associated with using sellfy for eCommerce. Once you compare these benefits to what you get with other platforms such as Shopify, you should find that it is worth your time to consider sellfy for your business. #9720. Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account

You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.

Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.

If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:

If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.

Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.

You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.

You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.

Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.

To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.

Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.

Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.

#9719. Your AI Agent Is Only as Reliable as the Blockchain State It Observes

AI Engineer and Enterprise Architect passionate about building scalable AI systems and production-ready agentic platforms. I write about AI.

AI Engineer and Enterprise Architect passionate about building scalable AI systems and production-ready agentic platforms. I write about AI.

AI Engineer and Enterprise Architect passionate about building scalable AI systems and production-ready agentic platforms. I write about AI.

An AI agent can make a perfectly reasonable decision and still get things wrong. Imagine an agent managing a crypto wallet. It checks the balance, reviews a transaction request, verifies that the amount is within the permitted limit, and prepares a transfer. Everything looks fine. The agent has followed its instructions, the calculations are correct, and the transaction appears to satisfy the application's rules.

But there is a problem. Another transaction has already moved some of the funds, and the application's internal balance has not been updated yet. The agent is working with yesterday's reality, even though the data it received looks legitimate.

This is the kind of problem that interests me when thinking about production AI systems. We spend a lot of time discussing better models, retrieval quality, context windows, and tool calling. Those things matter, but they do not solve a more basic problem: what happens when the information an agent relies on no longer reflects the system it is operating in?

Blockchain applications make this problem particularly interesting. Data moves through RPC providers, event subscriptions, indexers, databases, and caches before it reaches the application that needs it. Every component has its own timing and failure modes. By the time an AI agent uses that information, the underlying blockchain state may have changed.

The agent does not necessarily know that. It can only work with the information available to it. An AI agent is only as reliable as the state it observes and the system's ability to keep that state accurate.

This is not just a problem for crypto trading bots. It matters anywhere an autonomous system uses blockchain data to make decisions, including treasury management, decentralised finance, token transfers, and smart contract automation.

Let's start with something simple. A user transfers tokens from one wallet to another. The blockchain records the transaction, and a corresponding event can be emitted by the token contract. An application listens for that event and updates its database so that the user's portfolio reflects the change.

In an ideal world, the event arrives once, gets processed immediately, and the database always reflects the latest state.

Real systems are rarely that tidy. The same event might be delivered more than once. An indexing service might fall behind. A network interruption might delay processing. Two workers might process related events in the wrong order. A block that the application previously observed might later be replaced during a chain reorganisation.

None of these situations necessarily means the blockchain itself is broken. The problem is that the application can build an incorrect picture of the blockchain from the information it receives.

An event tells us that something happened within a particular chain of history. Application state is the result of interpreting those events, applying business rules, and maintaining a representation of the current situation.

Those are two different things. Consider an application that maintains token balances by adding incoming transfers and subtracting outgoing transfers. If it processes an incoming transfer twice, its internal balance increases twice even though the wallet received the tokens only once. The event can be genuine. The processing can still be wrong.

Now introduce an AI agent that uses the application's balance to decide whether it can execute a payment. The agent may receive an incorrect balance, calculate the requested amount correctly, and produce a transaction that passes the checks it was given.

The failure did not begin with the model's reasoning. It began with the state supplied to the model. This distinction is important because improving the model will not fix a broken state pipeline. The application needs to establish whether the information it provides is trustworthy before asking the agent to act on it.

Consider a hypothetical treasury agent who handles routine payments. Its application maintains an internal balance of 2,000 tokens. A transfer of 600 tokens is submitted from the wallet. The blockchain processes the transfer, but the event consumer has not yet updated the database.

Meanwhile, the agent receives a request to transfer another 1,700 tokens. The agent queries the database, sees a balance of 2,000 tokens, and concludes that the payment is affordable. Its reasoning may be completely correct based on the information it received. But the actual available balance may now be only 1,400 tokens.

The application has given the agent a number without making clear that the number represents an earlier state. A different failure could produce the opposite result. If an event is missed, the application might understate the balance and reject a legitimate payment.

Both problems come from the same assumption: that receiving and processing blockchain events automatically guarantees accurate application state. It doesn't.

For a read-only assistant, an incorrect balance may result in a misleading answer. For an agent that can initiate transactions, the same discrepancy can lead to a financial action that cannot easily be reversed.

That changes how we should approach state management. It should not be treated as a background implementation detail. It needs to be part of the reliability controls surrounding the agent.

There are several common failure modes worth understanding before designing the solution.

Event consumers sometimes retry work when acknowledgements are delayed, network connections fail, or a service restarts. If the application applies the same business operation every time it receives a message, a retry can create a duplicate effect.

A blockchain event can usually be identified using a combination of fields such as the chain ID, block hash, transaction hash, and log index. These fields can help the application recognise that it has already processed a particular event.

However, checking whether an event has been seen is not enough if the check and the resulting database update can happen independently. Two workers might receive the same event simultaneously, and both apply it. The application needs a concurrency-safe way to record the event and apply its effect.

Imagine an application processing a deposit followed by a withdrawal. If the withdrawal is processed first, a balance projection that relies on sequential updates may temporarily or permanently become incorrect.

Some events can be processed independently. Others require ordering guarantees or version checks. The important decision is whether the application's state model can tolerate reordering. If it cannot, the consumer must enforce the required ordering or rebuild the state from a reliable reference.

Indexers make blockchain data easier to query by turning low-level events into structured information. They are useful, but they are still processing systems with their own progress and latency.

An indexer can return a successful response while remaining behind the relevant chain state. This becomes especially problematic when an agent combines information from different sources. A wallet balance might come from a recent RPC call, while liquidity data comes from an indexer that has not yet processed the latest blocks.

Both responses may be valid for their respective observation points, yet the combined view may no longer describe a consistent situation.

Some blockchain networks can replace previously observed blocks before the relevant state reaches the required finality threshold. If an application has already applied events from a displaced block, its internal state may contain effects that no longer belong to the canonical chain history.

The application needs a way to identify affected records and reverse or rebuild the relevant projection. Treating every observed event as permanently final is not sufficient for systems that depend on accurate chain history.

Two workers might read the same database balance, calculate different updates, and then overwrite each other's changes.

This is a familiar distributed-systems problem known as a lost update. It can happen even when the blockchain events are genuine and delivered correctly. The database and processing architecture need appropriate transaction boundaries, locking, version checks, or other concurrency controls to prevent it.

These failures have different causes, but they all demonstrate why event delivery and state correctness must be treated as separate concerns.

If I were designing this system, I would separate event ingestion, state processing, validation, agent reasoning, and transaction execution. The goal would not be to introduce as many services as possible. It would be to make each responsibility clear enough that a failure in one stage does not silently corrupt everything that follows. Here is the basic flow:

The event listener captures changes from the blockchain. Durable storage preserves enough information to recover from processing failures. The event processor handles duplicates and applies changes according to the application's consistency rules.

The state layer maintains a queryable representation of the data. A reconciliation process checks whether that representation still agrees with an appropriate authoritative source. Only then does the agent use the information to propose an action. Before the action is executed, the system validates the assumptions that matter for that transaction. Once execution is complete, it verifies the result and updates the workflow state.

A small application might implement several of these responsibilities within a single service. A larger application may separate them into different components. The important part is the sequence and the guarantees, not the number of boxes in the architecture diagram.

One of the most useful techniques in event-driven systems is idempotency. An operation is idempotent when repeating the same logical operation does not create an additional unintended effect.

For blockchain event processing, the application can construct an event identity and use it to prevent the same event from being applied more than once. Here is a simplified Python example:

This illustrates the pattern rather than a complete production implementation. The storage layer must ensure that applying the event and recording it as processed are atomic, or otherwise protected against concurrent workers.

A database uniqueness constraint combined with a transaction is one common approach. Without such protection, two workers could both check for the event, both conclude that it is new, and both apply the change. There is another limitation worth mentioning. Including the block hash in the event identity helps distinguish events from different block histories, but it does not automatically handle chain reorganisations.

If a previously processed block is displaced, the application still needs to invalidate or reverse the state derived from that block. Idempotency prevents duplicate effects. It does not guarantee that an event remains part of the canonical chain.

That distinction is easy to miss when reliability patterns are treated as universal solutions rather than controls for specific failure modes.

Many applications store a balance or a position without recording enough information to explain how the value was produced. That works until something goes wrong.

Suppose an agent reads a balance of 1,250 tokens. An engineer investigating a later failure needs to know whether the balance came from a recent chain query, a cached response, or an indexer that was several blocks behind. The number alone cannot answer that question. I would associate a critical state with metadata describing its origin and processing history. Depending on the application, this might include the chain ID, block number, block hash, indexing checkpoint, projection version, and last successful reconciliation. For example:

These values are illustrative. A timestamp alone does not prove freshness, and the status should only be marked as verified after a defined validation procedure has succeeded.

For a system that depends on a particular chain history, the block hash is also useful because different blocks can exist at the same height. This metadata makes it possible to ask better questions. Which state did the agent observe? How far had the indexer progressed? Which version of the processing logic produced the value? Had the application reconciled the projection against an appropriate reference?

It also helps distinguish between historical information and the current state. An agent might need historical balances to explain how a portfolio changed over time. That information can remain useful indefinitely as historical evidence. It should not automatically be reused as the current balance for a new transaction.

The application needs to understand what a value represents and whether it remains suitable for the task at hand.

Even a carefully designed event processor can encounter missed updates, software defects, or unexpected infrastructure failures. Reconciliation gives the application a way to detect when its internal state no longer agrees with the relevant blockchain state. For a simple token balance, the application might compare its local projection with a balance obtained through an appropriate contract query. For a more complex lending position, it may need to query several contract values and reproduce the protocol's calculations.

The comparison must use equivalent state references. A local projection processed through block 100 may legitimately differ from a query against block 105 because additional transactions occurred in the meantime.

The application should first establish which blocks the projection has processed and which state the comparison represents. If a discrepancy is found, the system can investigate the event history, replay events from a known checkpoint, or rebuild the projection. It should not blindly overwrite the local value with a new query result without understanding the difference.

Reconciliation also needs to reflect the application’s risk profile. A reporting dashboard may tolerate some indexing delay. An agent preparing a high-impact transaction may require a more current state check before it is authorised to proceed.

This does not mean every model call needs to trigger a full reconciliation. A more practical design uses efficient projections for ordinary analysis and stronger validation at the point where a consequential action is authorised. That balance keeps the system usable without treating performance as a reason to ignore state integrity.

State management becomes even more important when an AI agent submits a transaction and does not receive a clear response. Imagine the agent sends a transaction through an RPC provider. The request times out. The agent does not know whether the transaction reached the network. If it assumes that the transaction failed and immediately submits another one, it could create an unintended duplicate operation.

A timeout tells us that the response was not received within the expected period. It does not prove that the underlying operation never happened. The application needs a durable transaction record that survives agent restarts and uncertain network conditions. That record should track the transaction hash when available, chain ID, sender, nonce, where applicable, submission attempts, observed receipts, and current lifecycle status.

The lifecycle might move through states such as proposed, validated, authorised, submitted, included, confirmed, and verified. An uncertain submission should have its own explicit state rather than being silently marked as failed. When a timeout occurs, the recovery process should inspect the original transaction and reconcile its status before deciding what to do next. A transaction might still be pending. It might have been included in a block. It might have reverted. It might have been replaced by another transaction using the same nonce. Those outcomes require different responses.

The agent's conversational memory should not be the authoritative source of transaction status. That status belongs in a durable application state, backed by the available transaction and receipt evidence. This is the same principle that applies to other autonomous workflows: a system must distinguish between an operation that failed and an operation whose outcome is not yet known.

This is where blockchain state management connects directly to my interest in context engineering. An agent's context is often treated as information assembled from documents, databases, tools, and memory. But context quality depends on more than relevance. The information must also be suitable for the decision the agent is about to make. A retrieved balance can be relevant but outdated. A protocol event can be accurate but incomplete. A stored transaction status can describe an earlier stage of execution.

If the agent cannot distinguish these conditions, it may reason correctly from information that should no longer be trusted. I would separate the workflow into three stages.

Observe. Retrieve state with enough metadata to establish its source, relevant block reference, and validation status.

Decide. Allow the agent to interpret the validated context and propose an action.

Authorize. Recheck critical assumptions and policy constraints before allowing the action to execute.

Suppose an agent prepares a swap based on a particular liquidity observation. The pool changes while the agent is reasoning. The proposal may no longer satisfy the conditions under which it was created. The runtime should detect that the relevant assumptions have expired and require fresh validation. It should not simply ask the model whether it is still confident. Confidence does not establish that the blockchain state remains unchanged.

This separation allows the agent to focus on interpreting goals and proposing actions, while the application remains responsible for state integrity and authorisation. It also makes the system easier to test. We can evaluate the agent's planning separately from the controls that prevent an invalid proposal from reaching execution. A capable agent should make useful decisions. A reliable application should know when those decisions are no longer safe to act upon.

A state-management design should be tested under failure conditions, not only against a clean stream of events. I would build a test suite that deliberately introduces duplicate delivery, delayed events, out-of-order processing, indexer lag, database concurrency conflicts, and uncertain transaction submissions. The system should demonstrate that it can detect these conditions and either recover or stop safely.

Ordering rules are enforced, or the state is reconciled

Stale data is identified before a sensitive action

The affected projection is invalidated or rebuilt

Concurrency controls prevent lost updates

The original transaction is reconciled before retrying

A balance differs from an authoritative state

The discrepancy is flagged, and the proposal is revalidated

These tests should be reproducible in a local environment or controlled test network. I would also measure duplicate suppression, projection divergence, reconciliation recovery time, unresolved transaction frequency, and the number of invalid proposals that reach the execution boundary.

For high-impact actions, the goal should be to prevent known state-integrity violations from resulting in unauthorised execution. The precise thresholds depend on the application. A reporting service and an autonomous treasury system should not necessarily have the same latency or consistency requirements. What matters is that the requirements are explicit and that the tests demonstrate whether the implementation meets them.

Even with good event processing and reconciliation, failures can still occur. Engineers need to understand when the application has stopped representing the state it claims to represent. For every important projection, I would monitor its processing checkpoint, indexing lag, last successful reconciliation, and number of events awaiting processing.

For every consequential agent decision, I would preserve the relevant observation references, projection version, policy result, and transaction lifecycle identifier. This makes it possible to trace an incorrect decision back to the stage where the state became unreliable.

Was an event never processed? Did two workers apply the same update? Did the indexer fall behind? Did the agent reuse an outdated observation? Did the execution layer fail to revalidate the balance? These are different problems, and the system should provide enough evidence to distinguish them.

Observability and state management serve different purposes. State management determines how the application constructs and maintains its view of reality. Observability helps engineers detect and explain when that view becomes unreliable. Together, they make the system easier to operate and safer to change.

As AI agents move into applications that can transfer assets, execute smart contracts, and manage decentralised workflows, the quality of their decisions will depend heavily on the state presented to them. A blockchain event may be valid. An indexer may return a successful response. A database query may complete without error. Yet the combined application state can still be incorrect.

That is why reliable autonomous systems need more than capable models. They need idempotent event processing, versioned state projections, reconciliation, chain-aware recovery, durable transaction lifecycles, and execution-time validation. These practices are not unique to blockchain, but blockchain makes their importance particularly clear.

The objective is not to eliminate every delay or force every application to wait for the strongest possible confirmation. It is to understand the guarantees required for each operation, detect when those guarantees are no longer satisfied, and prevent unsafe actions from proceeding.

For me, this is the broader connection between context engineering and distributed-systems reliability. An agent's decision is only as good as the information it receives, and that information is only useful when the application understands what it represents.

Reliable AI is not just about making better decisions. It is about ensuring that decisions are based on a trustworthy state and preventing them from being executed when that state can no longer be trusted. That is the engineering work that needs to happen before autonomous agents can be trusted with more consequential responsibilities.

How to Trace AI Agent Decisions Across Blockchain Transactions

AI Engineer and Enterprise Architect passionate about building scalable AI systems and production-ready agentic platforms. I write about AI.

#9716. Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:

MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d

Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

You can make compression proportional to document length:

With pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:

This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:

Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

If you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:

L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​

The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives update the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:

CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

The poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

The complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:

The script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

You can also train on a cloud GPU with Hugging Face Jobs. Install the CLI and log in with a token that can run Jobs and upload models:

This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

You can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:

In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:

Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

Sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

The default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:

The pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

You can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:

Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

At the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:

If the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

MultiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

#9715. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing.

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. If you're writing fiction, you may find Grammarly's insistence on "Conciseness" annoying. They seem to want to take the soul out of your writing, which is fine for a corporate report or technical manual, but not for your Great American Novel.- Grammarly pushes features on users that are not ready for prime time. On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9713. How We Used Real Support Tickets to Gate LLM Agent Releases

Founding PM at a European B2B parts marketplace. Writes about AI agents in production, search, and killing products on time.

Founding PM at a European B2B parts marketplace. Writes about AI agents in production, search, and killing products on time.

Founding PM at a European B2B parts marketplace. Writes about AI agents in production, search, and killing products on time.

If you have put an LLM agent anywhere near customers, you already know the uncomfortable part. You can see everything it does, and you still don’t know whether it’s right.

Our team had full tracing on our support triage agent from day one. We could replay any ticket, read every tool call, watch it reason. What we didn’t have, for the first six weeks, was any way to say before a release whether the new version was better or worse than the old one. We found out in production, when return requests started landing in the wrong queue.

This post is the practical version of how we fixed that: how a 14-engineer team with no ML specialists built an eval set that now gates every change to the agent. Nothing here needs a platform. It needs a spreadsheet, a few hours from the person who knows the domain, and the discipline to run it every time.

The first instinct is to write test cases. Don’t. Pull real inputs.

We exported about 200 recent support tickets, removed anything with personal data, and gave them to our support lead, the person who had been answering them by hand for two years.

She picked 40 that between them covered the shapes of question we actually get: where is my order, is this part compatible, I want to return this, the invoice is wrong, I never received it, plus a handful of ambiguous ones where even a human would hesitate.

Forty sounds small. It is small. It was also enough to catch the two failures that mattered in the first month, and small enough that one person could label it in an afternoon, which is the real constraint.

An eval set nobody maintains is worse than none, because it gives you false confidence.

For each ticket we recorded three things.

For a where-is-my-order ticket, the reply must cite the last carrier scan and must not say “on its way” unless that scan exists.

We did not write a model answer. Grading against a model answer makes the eval about wording, and wording is the thing LLMs are good at. The decisions are what go wrong.

The returns failure came from exactly this gap. Our first labels had the routing decision but our examples all used the word “return”. Customers wrote “can I send this back” and “it’s not the one for my machine”, the agent filed them as general enquiries, and because tickets-answered was going up nobody looked.

Those misrouted tickets are now their own block in the set, and anything with return intent routes to a person regardless of what the model thinks.

Routing and hand-off decisions are checked by code: did the agent pick the labelled queue, yes or no. That’s a script and it runs in seconds.

The content checks, must-contain and must-not-claim, we grade with a second model call that sees the reply and the labels and returns a pass or fail with a one-line reason. We spot-check about a fifth of those by hand every run, because a grader that nobody audits drifts just like the agent does.

The whole set runs in under two minutes. That matters more than it sounds.

If it took an hour, it would run weekly. Because it takes two minutes, it runs on every prompt change, every model switch, every new tool, and the result is posted to the channel where the change was proposed.

The number everyone looks at is routing accuracy on the 40, and the rule is simple: it does not ship if that number goes down.

The product manager, not the engineers, owns the set. That was the real shift.

Before, I wrote specs describing behaviour and engineers interpreted them. Now I write the test set and the pass criteria, and the agent’s output is graded against it. It is a different job.

A spec is an act of imagination about something that doesn’t exist. An eval is an act of judgment about outputs that do, and it forces you to decide, in advance and in writing, what correct means for your customers.

It also changed how we scope. Each new workflow we hand to an agent starts with its eval set, funded before the feature.

We said no to the next several agent ideas because nobody had time to build the set, and that was the right call.

In the first months, review load grew faster than drafting time fell, and velocity didn’t move until we narrowed scope to three workflows and gave reviewers a one-page checklist.

Most teams I talk to have observability and no evals. They can watch the agent fail. They can’t catch it first.

The fix does not need a platform or a research team. It needs forty real inputs, the person who knows the answers, three labels per input, and a two-minute script that runs every single time.

Build that before the next feature, not after the next incident.

Founding PM at a European B2B parts marketplace. Writes about AI agents in production, search, and killing products on time.

#9711. BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

🤗 Model (safetensors)  |  📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4)

We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement.

BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).

Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.

We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.

Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).

Learning from rules and environments (RL stages)

Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.

The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.

Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.

BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.

Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).

BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.

Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).

On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.

Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).

BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.

Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.

Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):

It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.

BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.

BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.
