#9710. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9709. The Next Pandemic May Not Infect Humans

I build systems that scale and lead teams that ship.

I build systems that scale and lead teams that ship.

I build systems that scale and lead teams that ship.

We keep connecting software and giving AI agents more room to act. I think that changes how attacks can spread.

October has been a rough month for anyone trying to keep software secure.

PHP disclosed critical vulnerabilities. Node.js released security fixes, with the most serious rated High. Zeabur reported an intrusion involving leaked internal credentials, and LiteLLM's official release pipeline published a compromised package and container images.

By the end of the month, Polymarket had reported a third-party compromise affecting its international platform, and Binance had disclosed a theft of about $6.3 billion.

These are separate incidents. Some are vulnerability disclosures, and some are actual breaches. I haven't seen evidence that they were coordinated, or that AI agents caused all of them.

Looking at them together, though, I keep noticing how much of our security depends on other people's systems staying trustworthy. A package comes through the official release channel. A cloud platform holds credentials for infrastructure we run. A third-party script runs on a page where people manage money. Most days those connections work, so we stop thinking about them.

Now, we're adding AI agents that read across those systems and act on what they find. I'm less worried about whether an agent can be tricked once. I'm more worried about whether it can pass the trick on.

In 2017, WannaCry spread through vulnerable computers and disrupted hospitals, businesses, and public services. NotPetya started with a compromised software update and spread through corporate networks, causing damage far beyond its first targets.

Neither attack had to reach every victim on its own. They moved through connections that already existed.

Modern software has a lot of those. Even a small application can rely on hundreds of packages, an outside login provider, several APIs, cloud infrastructure, and an automated deployment pipeline. A developer may depend on a package they have never read because some other package needs it.

That isn't necessarily careless. No team can build and audit everything it uses, and shared software is a big reason small teams can ship anything at all.

The cost is that when a trusted component fails, the damage can reach systems whose owners never chose to trust the original source.

AI didn't create this problem. It does change how much software we produce, how fast we connect it, and how much those connections are allowed to do.

Someone with little programming experience can now describe an application to a coding agent and have something working in an afternoon. I get why people are excited. An idea that used to stay in a notebook can turn into a working tool before dinner.

Trouble starts when "it works" gets treated as "I understand what was built."

An agent can pick dependencies, write authentication logic, configure database access, and set deployment permissions along with the parts you can see. Those choices still need review, even if the person accepting them didn't realize they were choices.

A missing authorization check won't show up on any screen. A credential can have far more access than the app needs. An unnecessary dependency won't make a single test fail.

Experienced engineers miss these things too, and handwritten code isn't automatically safer. What's different now is volume. We can produce a lot more code, and the attention available to review it hasn't grown at the same rate.

Put simply, writing software is getting cheaper faster than understanding, securing, and maintaining it.

For a prototype that never leaves a laptop, that may be fine. For an app holding customer data, or a tool wired into a company's internal systems, somebody inherits the gap, usually whoever has to run it later.

Attackers get the same discount. AI can help them generate variations of malicious code, adapt scripts to different environments, and automate parts of their research. Most attempts will still fail, but each one costs less, so they can try more.

It's tempting to compare this to biological mutation, where more variations mean more chances that one survives. The comparison only goes so far, and a generated variation is often worse than the original. My point is narrower. If experimenting gets cheaper for attackers while careful review stays expensive for defenders, defense gets harder.

Writing code is only part of the change. We're also giving agents terminals, browsers, repositories, cloud dashboards, and production credentials.

An assistant that explains an error is useful. One that investigates the error, changes a configuration, and deploys a fix is more useful, and it's now working with authority that used to belong to a person.

Take a hypothetical cloud operations assistant. It reads logs, checks deployments, and can make a limited set of changes to restore service. One day, an attacker plants text in a log entry, written to look like an operational instruction.

The log is meant to be evidence. If the agent reads that line as an instruction, the attacker has gotten something done without ever logging into the dashboard.

How bad that is depends on the assistant's permissions. If it can only read logs, not much happens. If it can pull secrets, change firewall rules, or trigger deployments, the same mistake gets serious quickly.

The agent doesn't need to want anything harmful. It can be doing its best to finish the task it was given and still use legitimate access for something nobody approved.

This reaches beyond software companies. Hospitals, logistics providers, banks, and manufacturers all rely on software for everyday work. An outage in a scheduling or dispatch system can affect people who have never heard of the agent that changed it.

Access to a business application isn't automatically access to a factory's control systems, and those boundaries matter. But nobody needs to imagine an agent taking over a power plant. Breaking the systems people use to coordinate their work can already cause real harm.

Prompt injection happens when an agent treats untrusted content as instructions instead of as material to work on. The content might sit in an email, a document, a web page, or a tool response.

What gets less attention is that agents also write content other agents will read.

Imagine a support assistant reading a malicious email. It creates an internal ticket summarizing the issue and carries the malicious instruction into that ticket. A second assistant reads the ticket to investigate it. If that assistant makes the same trust mistake, the attack has reached another system through normal work.

That example is hypothetical, but the idea has been tested. In Morris II, researchers built self-replicating malicious prompts that spread between experimental AI email assistants. The experiments ran in a lab, and they don't show that anything like this is spreading in real applications.

Copying a prompt doesn't make it a worm. For an attack to keep moving, the receiving agent has to follow it, has to have somewhere to write, and has to pass along something that still works on the next reader. Tight permissions or a well-enforced trust boundary can break that chain at any step.

What makes this kind of carrier unusual is that the email or ticket may contain no executable malware at all. It's an ordinary object moving through an ordinary workflow, and the harm only shows up when a reader gives part of it more authority than it deserves.

The compromised agent might keep doing most of its job well. It answers questions, summarizes documents, and closes routine tickets. One bad action among a hundred good ones doesn't look much like a system that has been taken over.

If the instruction ends up in a shared document or in an agent's saved context, it can be picked up again later. A summary might drop it, or it might keep exactly the part the attacker cared about. Rewriting doesn't reliably make it stronger, and it doesn't reliably make it safe either.

I'm honestly not sure we would notice this kind of compromise while the work still looked productive.

We've spent decades building the digital equivalent of an immune system.

Antivirus software, firewalls, endpoint detection, sandboxing, access controls, vulnerability scanners, and incident response procedures all grew out of earlier generations of threats.

We still need all of it. AI agents just bring a problem these tools weren't really built for.

A document can be perfectly safe to open and still contain instructions that steer an AI assistant. A tool response can contain no malicious code and still try to redirect an agent's decisions.

So on top of spotting dangerous software, we now have to notice when untrusted information starts being treated as authority.

Telling an agent not to follow instructions found in documents helps, but it isn't a security boundary, and the model shouldn't be the only thing making that call.

Most of our existing immune system learns from infections that have already happened. Someone catches a piece of malware, pulls out a signature or a behavior pattern, and defenses get updated to recognize it next time. Then it's detect, quarantine, and clean up.

That works when malicious code looks similar from one attack to the next. It works much less well when the attack is a sentence that can be phrased differently every time and tucked into an ordinary email or ticket. There may be no stable pattern to match.

I think agents will need something closer to reactive armor, meaning defensive agents that watch other agents while they work. They would flag an assistant that suddenly asks for credentials it has never needed, tries to send data somewhere new, or starts repeating the same odd instruction across tickets. Then they would act on their own, by pausing the agent, revoking its access, isolating its outputs, or pulling in a human before anything else happens.

Basically, AI defending against AI. When agents are constantly reading and acting on each other's output, no person can review every step, so some of the defense has to move as fast as the attack.

The armor has a weak spot of its own. A defensive agent also reads what the attacker wrote, and if it can be talked out of raising the alarm, it's one more target. It can't rely on judgment alone. Underneath it, there still have to be hard limits on what each agent is allowed to do, a record of where each instruction came from, and a list of actions that always need a separate check.

Most of those limits are ordinary engineering. An assistant that summarizes tickets shouldn't be able to change production infrastructure. An assistant that deploys fixes should only reach the systems it actually needs. Sending data outside the organization or expanding access should require a separate check, not just a convincing explanation from the agent asking for it.

These controls add friction, and some automation will look less impressive in a demo. I think that's a fair price, because the more an agent can do, the further its mistakes can travel.

Then there's recovery, which I think matters even more.

If a traditional server is compromised, we can rebuild it from a trusted image, rotate its credentials, and restore verified data.

But what happens when an AI agent has spent weeks writing documents, updating databases, talking to other agents, and making decisions based on compromised information?

Cleaning up the original agent may not be enough, because the effects of its work may already be spread across the organization.

Some documents may need to be checked again. Some decisions may need to be reversed. Other agents may have pulled the compromised information into their own workflows.

Without records of what the agent read, whose authority it was acting under, and what it changed, recovery turns into guesswork.

Recovering from an infected agent might take more than deleting the malicious instruction. We may have to rebuild the whole chain of trust around it.

I don't expect millions of agents to suddenly turn against us. What worries me is millions of useful agents doing ordinary work with more access than they need, and with less separation between information and authority than we would accept anywhere else.

Meanwhile, apps keep getting cheaper to build and workflows keep getting easier to automate. Each new connection is useful on its own. Added together, they give one bad act of trust more ways to become someone else's problem.

This doesn't mean a digital pandemic is coming. A lab demonstration is not a forecast. An agent that reads malicious content isn't automatically compromised, and a compromised agent can't necessarily spread anything.

Still, we are actively building the conditions that would make that kind of spread possible. Our systems read each other's output, keep context around, hand off tasks, and act without a person checking each step.

If an outbreak like this happens, it probably won't look like computers crashing all at once. An assistant reads a normal-looking document, makes a change nobody asked for, and writes the same instruction into a ticket for the next assistant. The apps stay online while the damage moves through the work itself.

October already gave us plenty of examples of what misplaced trust can cost.

Before we connect agents to everything, I'd like to have a good answer for what happens when one of them trusts the wrong thing, and how we stop that mistake from turning into the next agent's instructions.

What Happens When Economic Growth No Longer Needs People?

I build systems that scale and lead teams that ship.

#9706. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9704. How to Loop a Video With FFmpeg (Count the Plays, Cut to an Exact Length, Check the Seam With pytest)

To loop a video with FFmpeg, put -stream_loop N before the -i it applies to. N is the number of extra plays, so -stream_loop 3 gives you four plays, -stream_loop -1 loops forever, and you stop the infinite version with -t. That is the whole trick; the rest of this post is about the three ways it quietly goes wrong and a small pytest suite that catches them.

Everything below was run on November 12, 2026 with Homebrew FFmpeg 9.0.1 on macOS against a real 10.04-second clip (720x1280, 24 fps, AAC audio): the public cat example from Voor's Bad Times AI page. Any short MP4 works the same way.

Loop a fixed number of times, no re-encode:

Loop to an exact length (re-encode so the cut lands on a frame, not on a packet):

Loop the picture under a longer soundtrack and end exactly when the soundtrack ends:

The option counts repeats, not plays. On the 10.04 s clip, -stream_loop 3 -c copy produced a 40.236 s file. If you want "play it three times", pass plays - 1. The wrapper below does that for you and refuses plays=0.

It is an input option and applies only to the -i that follows it. Put it after -i clip.mp4, right before the output name, and FFmpeg 9.0.1 refuses to run: "Option stream_loop ... cannot be applied to output url ... you are trying to apply an input option to an output file". With two inputs, only the one directly after -stream_loop loops; that is how the soundtrack command keeps the music playing once while the picture repeats.

FFmpeg's loop is a hard cut back to frame 0. To prove the restart is exact, I decoded the frame just after the 10.04 s boundary of a 2-play file and compared it with frame 0 of the source: PSNR was inf (identical). The last frame of pass 1, compared with frame 0, scored 15.9 dB: a completely different picture. In this clip the cat ends with both paws on the lens and starts sitting back, so every loop shows a visible jump.

That is not a bug to fix with flags. If you need a seamless loop, the clip itself has to end where it began (or you crossfade the tail into the head, which changes the content). Measure it before you promise "seamless".

The 25 s soundtrack in the test is a generated sine tone, so the suite needs nothing but FFmpeg and the one clip.

Stream copy is fast and lossless but can only cut where packets end. For an exact length, or when the clip has only a keyframe at the start (this one does), re-encode.

The fixture is a real generated example from Voor's Bad Times AI page: one photo of a pet, baby or person turned into a 10-second 9:16 "argument with the camera" clip with the song included. On November 12, 2026 the page quoted 439 credits for one clip (Pet routine selected, Public · watermarked). If you want your own short clip to loop on a profile page or a Story, you can make a Bad Times clip from one photo and run the commands above on the MP4 you download.

#9702. 51 Thanksgiving dessert recipes for a sweet holiday: From cookies to cake — and of course, plenty of pie.

Of course, we had to start with pumpkin pie. This is a rich, well-spiced pie, thanks to a powerful punch of ginger, cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, and black pepper. Two hints for a better result: Mix the filling a day in advance to give the spices a chance to bloom, and be sure to remove the pie from the oven while the center is still wobbly, as overcooking it will cause the filling to crack.

Want even more spice in your pumpkin pie? This spice-forward recipe is for you. Using powerful Vietnamese cinnamon — with its more robust flavor profile — gives the pie an even spicier kick. Meanwhile, the filling is super silky-smooth thanks to a few tablespoons of corn syrup mixed in.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

With its retro vibe, this play on classic chiffon pie is noteworthy for its tender rye crust and its bright, light chiffon filling. The zesty cranberry curd and smooth, sweet Swiss meringue play beautifully together. And the gelatin helps the filling set just right so that once refrigerated, the pie can be sliced neatly. Tart and airy, this pie is an excellent counterpoint to a heavy feast.

Shop the recipe: Organic Medium Rye Flour

Intimidated by pie? Don't be! Our guide on How to Bake Pie has everything you need for a successful, stress-free bake.

This double-crusted beauty is generously filled with sweet-tart apples and spiced with cinnamon, nutmeg, and allspice. But the real secret to its flavorful filling is boiled cider, one of our favorite fall ingredients. The sticky tart-sweet syrup adds an extra depth of apple flavor to make this classic pie stand out from the crowd.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Boiled Cider and Instant ClearJel

This unusual method for baking apple pie caught our eye years ago, when a reader sent it via e-mail. But it’s not just a stunt: Baking a pie in a paper grocery bag gives you a beautifully golden brown, perfectly cooked pie, with toothsome yet tender apples (which soften better thanks to the steam trapped by the bag) beneath a streusel topping.

This beloved pie is made much like pumpkin pie, but with mashed sweet potatoes for nuanced flavor and heavy cream for an especially rich custard. Top it with toasted molasses meringue (if you want the pie to be reminiscent of the classic yams and marshmallow dish served at Thanksgiving), or for a simpler option, with freshly whipped cream. (And for a more unconventional version, try this striking Purple Sweet Potato Pie.)

This traditional pie doesn’t use corn syrup — instead, it’s sweetened entirely with brown sugar. The filling is silky smooth, and the pecans on top toast nicely as the pie bakes. Be sure to use high-quality vanilla extract for well-rounded flavor; an optional handful of chopped bittersweet chocolate is a nice addition, too.

If you’re intimidated by pie (or just don’t have time to chill and roll out pie dough) this easier version of pecan pie is for you. A buttery, brown-sugar shortbread crust cradles a gooey honey-sweetened pecan filling. These bars keep well for days, so they’re perfect for baking ahead of Thanksgiving.

This recipe takes classic pecan pie a step further by adding chocolate chips to the filling. The chocolate beautifully complements the pecans' nuttiness; if you choose bittersweet chocolate, it cuts the pie's overall sweetness, allowing all of the flavors to shine more brightly.

Shop the recipe: Guittard Bittersweet Chocolate Chips

Baker's tip: Make and freeze your pie crust early to get ahead on pie prep.

This creamy, decadent pie is positively bursting with maple flavor — be sure to use the best maple syrup you can find and a dash of natural maple flavor to enhance it. One bite of the brûléed maple sugar top and the silky-smooth filling will have you reconsidering your regular rotation of cream pies this Thanksgiving.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Maple Syrup and Natural Maple Flavor

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar. If you’re only in charge of dessert this year and want to flex a little, this recipe is an impressive (and tasty!) way to do so.

Shop the recipe: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice

Mash-up pies are an easy way to please your guests without making multiple pies. This recipe has the best of both worlds: a smooth layer of spiced pumpkin custard plus a rich pecan topping. It’s best made a day ahead so that the flavors can settle, plus there’s one less dish to worry about on Thanksgiving Day.

Shop the recipe: Adjustable Pie Crust Shield

Is there anything cuter than a mini Thanksgiving pie? Filled with a pre-cooked, perfectly spiced filling that’s enhanced with tart boiled cider, these bite-sized treats can be topped with a woven lattice or streusel.

This tart-sweet cake is easy to throw together — made with melted butter, the one-bowl batter is mixed by hand then poured directly over sugared cranberries. If you have cranberries leftover from making sauce or just want to highlight these seasonal berries in other ways, make this cake.

Shop the recipe: Pure Almond Extract and Sparkling Sugar

This stunning pumpkin swirl cake is more than just good looks: It also has a soft, plush texture, thanks to cake flour and sour cream, and a deep pumpkin flavor paired with fragrant vanilla. It starts with one base batter that gets flavored two ways, creating two distinct colors for a striking visual contrast when sliced.

For a more traditional dessert, try this pumpkin-y layer cake. It’s moist and slightly dense from the pumpkin purée, with a tangy cream cheese frosting and sticky caramel glaze.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting

In this unabashedly apple-forward apple cake, there are so many apple slices and so little batter, you’ll wonder how (and if) it will hold together. But never fear: As the batter rises in the oven, it knits those slices together to create a tender cake that’s almost creamy and custardy due to the abundance of fruit.

Shop the recipe: Almond Flour and Pure Almond Extract

The pumpkin and pumpkin-friendly spices (cloves, cinnamon, allspice) in this cake meld surprisingly well with the chocolate chips studded throughout. This dark, moist Bundt cake is rich enough to serve unfrosted, and it's just the ticket when you want to serve a dessert that's substantial, yet not too sweet, to finish your Thanksgiving meal. And it keeps well for days, so you can bake it early in the week to help prep ahead.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin-Chocolate Chip Cake

This golden cake is rich, moist, and subtly spiced to complement, rather than overshadow, the natural flavor of sweet potatoes. It also includes a crunchy pecan crust on both the top and bottom, along with a touch of maple syrup in the cake for sweetness. If you’re not a fan of pie, this sweet potato cake just may be the perfect Thanksgiving dessert.

Get the recipe: Pecan-Crusted Sweet Potato Pound Cake

Shop the recipe: Vermont Maple Syrup and Tube Pan

With a hidden swirl of coffee-flavored filling, this stunning cake adds an extra dimension to your holiday table. It’s like a pumpkin spice latte in dessert form — and also secretly whole wheat!

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake

Wondering how far ahead you can make your cake? Here's how long cake lasts in the fridge and at room temp.

This cake is an old favorite of our readers, with over 300 five-star reviews. It's a recipe where the whole is definitely more than the sum of the parts: The moist, semi-chunky cake is packed with four cups of apples, then spread with the frosting equivalent of brown sugar fudge. The whole thing comes together by hand in one bowl, so it also fits easily into your Thanksgiving prep.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

Shop the recipe: Apple Pie Spice and Vermont Boiled Cider

Why decide between cheesecake and pie when you can have both? This eye-catching two-toned recipe pairs custardy pumpkin pie with creamy cheesecake for a dessert that will satisfy everyone.

For an all-pumpkin Thanksgiving cheesecake, there’s this classic version, which transforms pumpkin pie into a silky, velvety filling. Because it needs to chill before serving, this cheesecake is an excellent candidate for baking a day ahead of Thanksgiving.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cheesecake with Gingersnap Crust

Shop the recipe: Vietnamese Cinnamon, Ginger, and Nutmeg

We did the testing: This is the best way to keep your cheesecake from cracking.

Top with maple- or bourbon-spiked whipped cream to dress it up for the holiday; details are in the recipe tips at the bottom of our Homemade Whipped Cream recipe.

For a fall-forward cheesecake, turn to this seasonal recipe. The texture of the filling is ultra-smooth and creamy, and the maple flavor is apparent, yet subtle — the secret is natural maple flavor paired with maple syrup. The pecan crust, meanwhile, is a nutty, salty counterbalance to the filling.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Maple Syrup and Natural Maple Flavor

If you’re looking for a celebratory yet unexpected dessert for your table, we recommend this recipe. A heavy pour of Irish whiskey cream liqueur (save some for your after-dinner coffee!) flavors the smooth, light filling, while silky chocolate ganache adorns the top. Oven space at a premium while you prep Thanksgiving dinner? This dessert is no-bake, so you can save some room in the cooking schedule.

With its burnished top and custardy interior, this cheesecake reimagines the classic with bold autumnal flair, thanks to golden pumpkin purée and warm spices.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This flourless cake is incredibly rich — like sliceable fudge sauce. A thick icing of chocolate ganache glaze takes it over the top, but if you want something a touch lighter after a heavy Thanksgiving feast, top it instead with a dusting of confectioners’ sugar and a spoonful of barely sweetened whipped cream.

Baker's tip: Make your whipped cream in a Mason jar, especially helpful if you're bringing dessert to someone else's home.

Shop the recipe: Callebaut Semisweet Chocolate Chips

This chocolate pie, with its flaky pastry crust and glistening, ruby-colored cranberry topping, is a non-traditional twist on Thanksgiving flavors. With a semisweet chocolate ganache, nutty whole-grain flour in the crust, and tangy fruit, it delivers a novel and enticing new holiday pie.

This pecan tart recipe is the more lavish, decadent cousin of a classic pecan pie. The pecans are enveloped in a rich, chewy caramel filling, and a blanket of velvety smooth chocolate ganache covers the top of the tart, lending it major candy bar vibes with a touch of sophistication.

Shop the recipe: Guittard Semisweet Chocolate Wafers

This nostalgic pie is the perfect combination of crispy crust, dense chocolatey filling, and ethereal whipped cream. The crust is prebaked, then filled with a generous amount of cooked, cooled chocolate filling. You can customize the chocolate flavor to your taste by using bittersweet, semisweet, milk chocolate, or any combination of these that you like.

But worry not: Despite being vegan, it has the fragrant spiced flavor of classic pumpkin pie.

Instead of eggs, this pie relies on cornstarch to bind the gooey filling; coconut cream, meanwhile, stands in for butter. With tons of toasty pecans bound together in a rich, sweet syrup and cradled in a flaky crust, it’s hard to believe this pie is vegan.

The secret is coconut: The pudding-like filling is made with both coconut cream and evaporated coconut milk for a rich texture that’s the perfect balance of set but still soft. #9699. CSV vs CSV UTF-8: the same rows in four encodings, byte by byte

Posted on Nov 12 • Originally published at csvlane.com

"CSV" and "CSV UTF-8" sound like two formats. They are the same format: CSV describes the rows and columns, UTF-8 describes how the characters are stored as bytes. The only other thing that differs is an optional three-byte mark at the start of the file.

To see exactly what changes, I saved the same three rows (Zoë Müller, José Peña, Chloé Dubois) in four encodings and read the bytes.

A CSV file on disk does not say which encoding it uses (RFC 4180 leaves the character set to a MIME parameter), so software guesses. A wrong guess gives one of two recognisable patterns:

The first can be undone by re-reading the original. If a program has already saved the file with replacement characters, those letters are gone from that copy.

Microsoft says a UTF-8 CSV opens normally in Excel if it was saved with the mark. Scripts are a different story. Python 3.9.6 with csv.DictReader:

Excel's own "CSV (Comma delimited)" and "CSV UTF-8 (Comma delimited)" both use commas; the name before the brackets is about the encoding. Microsoft's format table does not name an encoding for the plain one, so check a saved file rather than trusting the name.

The four test files, the full write-up and a browser tool that shows a file's encoding and saves UTF-8 with or without a BOM are on CSVLane. It runs in the browser tab, so the file is not uploaded.

This post was prepared with AI assistance and adapted from the original article on csvlane.com; the byte counts and Python results come from the test files linked there.

#9697. Yougov Publishes Scientific Validation of Its AI Twins and Challenges Industry To Set Research Stand

TechnologyWire (Technology Wire) is a tech newswire and press release distribution platform operated by MediaFuse LTD.

TechnologyWire (Technology Wire) is a tech newswire and press release distribution platform operated by MediaFuse LTD.

TechnologyWire (Technology Wire) is a tech newswire and press release distribution platform operated by MediaFuse LTD.

New York City, United States, November 10th, 2026/TechnologyWire/--YouGov, the international research and data analytics group, today published a white paper on one of the most transparent tests yet of one-to-one human-to-digital-twin simulation.

Rather than comparing aggregate results against public datasets, the groundbreaking research checked each AI twin individually against its own human.

Working with OriginalVoices, an AI platform specializing in simulation, YouGov built digital twins – LLM-based simulations of real people’s attitudes, which it calls “E-twins” – of 1,008 government ID-verified members of its proprietary panel. It then put the same new questions to both the E-twin and the real human respondent. Fully 69% of the panelists responded within 48 hours, giving a direct check on the accuracy of their E-twins. In day-to-day operations, this validation can be done in as little as an hour.

The Key Findings From Yougov’s AI Twins Testing:

YouGov says much of the evidence offered to date by simulators across the industry rests on publicly available datasets. Those questions may already sit in the training data of the underlying language models, so a twin can appear to know an answer it has simply absorbed – and respondents cannot be recontacted to verify the results. Aggregate comparisons can also mask twins that flatten towards the average or stereotype.

YouGov is calling on the industry to develop shared standards of verification and validation for defined use cases. It challenges all simulators to follow its lead in validating twins against their individual human, test them on unseen topics, publish their methods, show their misses and predict real-world outcomes in public.

Stephan Shakespeare, CEO and co-founder of YouGov: “The research industry is being transformed by AI in many ways but especially when it comes to simulation. Whether this is a dangerous development or a beneficial advance depends on whether clients can know if its outputs are reliable. I challenge everybody in the industry to work together to establish standards for verifying and validating simulated data. This white paper shows what we think these standards should involve - including the ability to validate simultaneously. If the industry wants simulation to be trusted by clients and the public, it needs to earn it and this can only be achieved through widely agreed standards.”

YouGov’s white paper also publishes the gaps future analysis will address. The current study did not measure a ceiling – how often a person repeats their own answer to the same question. A twin can't reasonably beat the person it copies: if panelists repeated their own rating 70% of the time, the twins' 58% exact-match rate would represent 83% of that ceiling. YouGov will test this in the next iteration of its research.

Read the full white paper: An evaluation of digital twins based on YouGov panel data

YouGov is a global research data and analytics group. Our mission is to offer unparalleled insight into what the world really thinks and does. With operations in the Americas, Mainland Europe, UK and Asia Pacific, we have one of the world's largest research networks.

Above all, YouGov is powered by reality. That stems from a unique panel of millions of registered members across 64 markets, encapsulating some 21 million shopping trips and millions of interconnected data points. Our unique approach to recruiting and engaging with our panel, combined with our state-of-the-art technology platforms, enables us to deliver real-world, real-time insights that lead to better decision-making and a competitive advantage for our clients.

As innovators and pioneers of online market research, we have a strong reputation as a trusted source of accurate data and insights. Testament to this, YouGov data is regularly referenced by the global press, and we are consistently one of the most quoted market research sources in the world.

For further information, visit yougov.com

#9696. Building Introworth: A Debt Feels Different When the Total Is Visible. What Worked, What Broke

Posted on Nov 12 • Originally published at onelifevibe.blogspot.com

A monthly payment is a terrible progress report. It stays the same while the balance moves, so a person paying a debt down can do everything right for months and still see no change in the number they look at most. A single monthly payment, repeated for a year, can feel like walking in place, even when hundreds of dollars of principal have already been paid.

The problem is not a lack of discipline. It is a lack of a visible total. A debt feels endless when it is only ever seen one payment at a time. It becomes a project with an end date when it is seen alongside every other balance: assets on one side, debts on the other, and the difference between them as the number that matters.

Introworth was built around that difference. Instead of opening to a list of accounts, it opens to a single net worth figure, with the assets and debts that make it up underneath. The order is deliberate. A list of accounts invites a person to check each balance in isolation. A single total invites a different question: is this number moving in the right direction, and how fast?

The design choice has a second effect. When the total is the main view, the individual accounts stop competing for attention. A savings account, a card balance, and a loan do not each need their own verdict. They need to be weighed together, because the total is the only figure that captures whether the overall position improved.

Most of the work was in making the total trustworthy. Balances are entered by hand, so the tool has to make a monthly update quick enough to repeat and hard to get wrong. If updating takes too long, the data goes stale. If it is too easy to mistype, the total lies. A net worth figure is only useful while a person still believes it, and belief depends on how easily the number can be checked.

Keeping the home screen to one number worked better than expected. People who had tried spreadsheets said the difference was not the arithmetic, which a spreadsheet does well, but the absence of clutter. There was nothing to maintain, no columns to fix, and no formulas to break. The total was there every time the page opened, and it either moved or it did not.

A fixed monthly review also worked. The same set of balances, updated on the same day each month, turned a chore into a routine. The review stayed short because the questions stayed the same: what is owed, what is owned, and has the gap moved the right way? Over several months, that routine produced something a spreadsheet rarely did: a continuous record of the total, month by month, in one place.

Showing debts and assets together, rather than in separate sections, worked as well. A debt paid down by $200 while savings fell by $200 is not progress, and the combined total makes that obvious. Separate views can hide the trade. A single total cannot, because it falls when money moves from savings to a card without reducing what is owed overall.

The first version tried to do too much with each account. It offered categories, notes, and per account targets, on the assumption that more detail would lead to better decisions. In practice, the extra fields slowed the monthly update and gave people reasons to put it off. Most of the detail was removed. What remained was the balance, the name, and whether it was an asset or a debt.

The second problem was the temptation to add charts. A graph of net worth over time sounds useful, and it is, but an early chart made small monthly changes look dramatic by scaling the axis to the range of the data. A $50 improvement looked like a steep climb. The axis was fixed to start at zero for the main view, so that a small gain looks small and a large gain looks large.

The third problem was subtler: the tool made it too easy to update balances without thinking. A quick update can become a habit of typing numbers without looking at them, and a mistyped balance can sit unnoticed for a month. A simple confirmation screen was added, showing the new total next to the previous total, so that an unexpected jump has to be acknowledged before it is saved.

Lead with the outcome number, not the activity numbers. Payments, logins, and updates are activity. The total moving in the right direction is the outcome, and it deserves the top of the screen.

Show competing items side by side before offering any recommendation. Most ordering advice becomes unnecessary once rates, balances, and minimums share one view.

Design the update ritual before designing the dashboard. A monthly, ten minute, never changing routine is what keeps the data fresh enough for the dashboard to mean anything at all.

The project behind these lessons is Introworth, which tracks assets and debts together so net worth can be followed as one number over time, rather than reconstructed from separate statements each month.

#9695. 17 apple dessert recipes for fall baking: Embrace the season with apple tarts, cookies, cakes, and more.

There’s an apple dessert for everyone. For the purists, there are lattice-topped pies and shingled galettes. For the non-traditionalists, there are caramel-frosted cakes and fritter-inspired loaves. And for apple lovers that hate cinnamon? Well, there are custardy cakes and classic French tarts. Ready to start baking with fall’s best fruit? Read on for our best apple dessert recipes.

There’s no shortage of apple in this cake — applesauce keeps things moist while boiled cider adds sharp, tangy fruit flavor. The cake is great on its own, but pair it with light, creamy Whipped Caramel Frosting, and you’ve got an irresistible baked version of a caramel apple (with none of the fears about your teeth).

Get the recipe: Whipped Caramel Apple Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vermont Boiled Cider

You only need one apple (and two people eager for an apple dessert) to make a pair of these adorable galettes. Half the apple is sliced, while the other half is grated, which creates a hidden layer of jam beneath the shingled slices. Flaky fruit tarts don’t get easier (or cuter!) than this.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

Get the recipe: Apple Cider Snickerdoodles

This super-easy one-bowl cake is loaded with chopped apples and walnuts, which give this moist, spiced cake heft and texture. The frosting, akin to a velvety brown sugar fudge, adds a textural counterpoint and an extra dimension of richness.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" x 13" pan

Cinnamon and apple go together like a flannel and a beanie, but this recipe one-ups that perfect pairing with the addition of cinnamon chips. Diced apple and melty pockets of cinnamon-sugar are also studded throughout these autumnal scones, which are then finished off with an extra-crunchy sugar coating.

Get the recipe: Fresh Apple Cinnamon Scones

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cinnamon Sweet Bits

Ribbons of gooey, cinnamon-scented apples are twisted throughout this striking enriched loaf. Beautiful to behold (and easier to make than you’d think), this braided babka would be a welcome addition to any Rosh Hashanah table or fall celebration.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

Spoiler alert: The eponymous secret ingredient in this special pie is boiled cider! Made by cooking down apple cider into a concentrate, a few drops deliver big apple flavor. When used in apple pies, it super-charges the fruit’s tart, tangy flavor, delivering a pie with over-the-top apple goodness.

Get the recipe: Secret Ingredient Apple Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider

If your go-to doughnut order is an apple fritter, this mash-up cake was made for you. The batter is made using the reverse creaming technique, which ensures a velvety crumb and tender texture. In each slice, there’s a filling and topping of cinnamon-dusted apples and a final drizzle of icy-white vanilla glaze. A slice rivals anything you can get at your local doughnut shop.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant ClearJel

This time of year, apples don't need much to make them shine. The paper-thin, crackly top layer of this cobbler highlights the juicy fruit beneath. It doesn’t need a lot of adornment, but a scoop of vanilla ice cream never hurt anything.

#9693. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9691. Stack Canaries on x64 Windows: Leaking and Patching the Birdy

If you read my last post on Return-Oriented Programming (ROP), you probably noticed a small detail in the vulnerable C code I provided. I left printf(username) in the binary and said, "We aren't exploiting that today though. That is a topic for another write-up."

In general we have been doing stack exploitation. This will only work if the stack in question doesn't have a tripwire which is a exactly what a stack canary is. For those unaware the name comes from back went miners would put a canary bird in a mine. If the bird died it served as an early warning that the cave was bad. The concept is similar here. If the stack canary is overwritten then something has gone wrong.

The stack canary itself is a random 64-bit value placed directly between your local variables and the saved return address. First the compiler will add a stub that generates the canary on a given function stack. It GCC it looks a bit like this:

When it has been generated it becomes pretty conspicuous:

Here it's about 16 bytes apart from the return address. This can vary depending on compiler and the program itself

Before the function returns, it checks the canary against a master copy stored somewhere else in the program. If you want to overwrite the return address (to exploit the stack) you have to overwrite the canary to get there. When you do overwrite the canary, another stub added at the end checks it. If it's been modified it immediately calls to kill the process.

To be a bit more technical here, it moves the canary to RCX, loads the pointer to the master canary value in RAX then dereference RAX to get the master canary and subtracts it by RCX. If both values are equal the zero flag is set and the je jumps to your proper function epilogue so function returns properly. If not, then the programs calls and just dies.

Here is the vulnerable code. Notice we have a format string vulnerability in the username, and a buffer overflow in the password:

To replicate this environment, compile it with the stack protector enabled, but leave ASLR and PIE off for now so we can isolate the canary: gcc main.c -o canary_vuln.exe -fstack-protector-all -no-pie

This is where format string leaks come in. printf uses multiple arguments, including an identifier for the type you want to print, such as %s, %d, or %p. If that identifier is missing and you add one, printf will just grab whatever is next on the stack and print it. For example:

%p. printed out a pointer with a . separating them. with this we can see the address of the program from the outside but we will need of lot of "%p." to read all the data we want

Alright. It's time to lock in because things are about to get serious. in the source code we can see that the username buffer has a size of 512. After doing the math we can fit "%p." (3 bytes) into 512 about 170 times. In our case that's enough to leak what we wanted but in some cases you might not be able to leak all of it and may need to be more creative like finding offsets to address you did leak. This is the full exploit code.

Keep in mind that the buf is the msfvenom payload from the last tutorial (which you should check if you haven't):

Of course you would need to find the offset (num of bytes) it would take to go from the password buffer to the canary. I just subtract the start of the buffer and canary address to get it the manual way.

Anyway, I got the ret_addrfrom simply checking it in debugger. Since I know what the value is I can find ret_index easily with python's .index() method then minus two since we know the canary is two address (16 bytes) before the return address in the stack. In a situation where you don't know the the address beforehand or it changes (cough ASLR cough), You would actually need to know the position that the return address is in which can be tedious.

And just like that, the canary is neutralized.

I highly recommend uncommenting the debug line and attaching a debugger to the process that the python script spawned. You should ideally attach to the first instruction of the at the end. It helps actually see what's happening and is useful if you complied the code yourself.

As ususal I'll post the github link to the source and the exe when it's uploaded.

Next time, we'll look at the final boss: ASLR and at the next writeup after the ASLR one we will add all protections (DEP, canary, ASLR) and bypass them in one binary. Until then tho, Bye and leave comment if you have questions. Always happy to help

#9688. Your TV Cable Is a 2.5 Gbps Network: How MoCA Saved My Three-Floor Home

Seasoned in Information Technology but still curious about: Cybersecurity, Programming, Networking, AI, IT management.

Seasoned in Information Technology but still curious about: Cybersecurity, Programming, Networking, AI, IT management.

Seasoned in Information Technology but still curious about: Cybersecurity, Programming, Networking, AI, IT management.

In this article, I will share my personal experience of getting in touch with and implementing MoCA (Multimedia over Coax Alliance), including why, how, which choices I made, and which mistakes to avoid. I hope that it can help anybody interested in starting on this path.

In 2024, I moved to an independent house built on three floors... plenty of room available and just an FTTC internet connection capped at more or less 70 Mbps. I did not have many exigencies in terms of devices and interconnectivity—just a couple of NAS units, a printer, a smart TV (at that time plugged directly into the router), some domestic appliances like smart bulbs, a pet feeder, and some video surveillance cameras. All these latter leaned on the 2.4 GHz SSID of my router. The most critical point was regarding my NAS units, which I decided to place on the upper floor along with the printer, and the best solution I found was just to set up a Wi-Fi mesh using an AP (TP-Link RE450). The Wi-Fi router was instead placed on the ground floor, thus the speed and the signal were quite poor, but with a slow FTTC, you almost don't notice it.

Finally, after a couple of years, FTTH was delivered to my city and I quickly decided to upgrade my slow internet connection; I was lucky anyway since a 2.5 Gbps line was available, to which I switched immediately.

And then... the situation became quite different. How can I take full advantage of this bandwidth and make it available in all my home? I suddenly discovered that at several points (especially on the upper floor) walls were obstructing the Wi-Fi signal so that I could not fully benefit from my router, which in turn is also capable of providing a Wi-Fi 7 signal; my internet provider released to my contract a ZTE ZXHN H6745 router which also features one 2.5 Gbps port and two Gbps ports, thus there is the room and the capability to distribute the signal in other ways than Wi-Fi.

After a quick check, I discovered that the Wi-Fi signal on the upper floor and in one bedroom located on an intermediate floor was decreased by 50% up to 85%, jumping from up to 1 Gbps in Wi-Fi 7 close to the router to 400-500 Mbps on the upper floor, while in the room with the NAS units I could just get barely 100-150 Mbps and even less in the aforementioned bedroom. This could be acceptable for many applications, but not, for example, when backing up my laptop or moving large files to/from the NAS units, and moreover, who knows about any future usages?

So, the first answer to this requirement must be obvious: set up a small LAN pulling cables up to your router, add Ethernet wall jacks whenever necessary, and a switch patched to your router which has, luckily, a port with proper speed. This was the first step and my first attempt.

First, I need to say that my home has several rooms, each of them equipped with phone and TV wall jacks. I counted in total 8 TV coax plugs (all working) and 7 RJ11 phone plugs (never tested and used, anyway they are there...) thus the first and less impactful option was to assess this spare infrastructure to enrich it with Cat.6 cables that could provide all the necessary speed and bandwidth. Fish-taping several times from all the wall jacks, I discovered that most of the plugs are connected to a daisy chain (see Picture 1), and this, of course, does not make things easier.

I could not locate the ending point for all the plugs since, in 3 cases, the electrician used the same conduits for the AC cables and the phone, and I preferred not to touch them. Given that, I could assess that probably (but for sure not easily) I could turn into Ethernet 4 out of 7 phone plugs using "normal" Cat 6 cables, thus not specific CEI-UNEL 36762 C-4 according to Italian regulations. Anyway, to make a cable arrive at the router, I had to pull it through three different plugs and this, although possible, is not a guarantee of success, not being an expert in this stuff.

Googling and posing questions to ChatGPT, I found out that even in cases in which standard cabling cannot be put in place, there are options that could work provided that other kinds of connectivity are available. In detail, there are MoCA and G.hn, which also use other media to make the Ethernet signal travel. Here below I'm reporting a synthetic prospect of the different solutions that can be chosen:

Extremely stable; high throughput (around 2.5 Gbps); low latency.

Requires MoCA-compatible splitters; adapters can be pricey.

Alternatives to MoCA in specific regions.

High speeds; often easier to find in some markets.

Not compatible with MoCA; interference issues if TV signals are present

Reuses old telephone wiring; avoids drilling.

Very sensitive to wire quality/age; lower speeds than coax.

Immune to electrical interference; "future-proof."

Requires pulling new plastic optical fiber through conduits.

Performance drops with distance and "noisy" appliances (fridges, chargers).

Table 1 -- Ethernet alternatives comparison (table contents generated by AI)

According to this table and taking into account a given limitation of G.hn (all adapters currently have just Gigabit ports, while MoCA 2.5 has 2.5 Gb ports... why choose G.hn?) I went to MoCA and I decided to implement the necessary adjustments to my TV network to ensure MoCA compatibility and max speed.

First of all, an assessment was necessary to point out the interventions to be done. The "AS WAS" situation is depicted in Picture 2:

The assessment brought me the following points:

Among these, some recommendations must be pointed out which I learned directly on my skin:

Always use F-type connectors and be very careful when screwing them onto the coaxial cables, especially avoiding gaps between the dielectric and the connector, and using the appropriate size of the connectors. I was forced in some cases to use 5 mm connectors instead of 7 mm, since not all the cables in the conduits have the same section, unfortunately.

All the spare ports in the tap and splitters must be correctly terminated (I used Fracarro CA75F components) to avoid impedance mismatch and then diffraction of the MoCA signal.

Adding the POE filter between the antenna and the Fracarro DE4-12 also improved my signal, although not strictly necessary, having a dedicated and private TV aerial. The model I bought is quite common in the US and took a long time to be delivered: PPC 2520A GLP-1G70CWWS, which should cut the MoCA signal off by 70 dB, quite good for this. For this component, if you have (like myself) a power supply injecting DC voltage to the amplifier in the aerial, the position of this filter is quite important since its internal components do not allow DC voltage to pass. I have placed it cascaded to the OUT of the power supply.

TV signal first... I have three TVs in my home and they must keep working regardless of all the changes.

Last but not least: if you want to reach the max speed, everything should be compliant with that speed. For this reason, I had to replace the GE switch serving the NAS with a pretty good BrosTrend 2.5 Gbps switch with 8 ports. This seems obvious, but sometimes it could be a pitfall.

You can see the AS WAS and the AS IS situations in the TV infrastructure in the above Pictures 3, 4, and 5 for the AS WAS and below, Pictures 6, 7, and 8 for the AS IS. Picture 9 is the AS IS schema of the current situation, whilst Pictures 10, 11, and 12 are showing the current iperf3 speed tests to one of my NAS units (equipped with 2.5 Gbps NICs) with my laptop connected to the NAS switch (Picture 10), connected via MoCA to the TV wall jacks in a bedroom (Picture 11), and the lowest speed in Picture 12.

Differences in speed between Pictures 11 and 12 are negligible and I got the same values for 5 TV plugs out of 7, thus I am pretty satisfied with this... The lowest value in the kitchen is due mostly to attenuation and partially to an IEC plug that I did not replace with Fracarro.

I got excellent performance from MoCA, improving the situation especially where the Wi-Fi signal is poor. In Picture 13 you can find also the comparison of Internet Speed Tests between MoCA and Wi-Fi in the intermediate bedroom, which has the poorest Wi-Fi signal in my home. The laptop is equipped with a Wi-Fi 6 NIC.

Some considerations about this project which gave me the possibility to increase my knowledge about RF signals and satisfied my curiosity about a technology that in Italy is almost ignored although widespread in other countries like US:

Wall Jack Keystones (7, Cat 6) for Bticino Magic

Router switch 2.5 Gbps (Brostrend 2.5 Gbps 5 ports)

NAS Switch 2.5 Gbps (BrosTrend 2.5Gbps Ethernet Switch 8 Ports )

NAS Switch 2.5 Gbps (BrosTrend 2.5Gbps Ethernet Switch 8 Ports )

Table 2 Comparison between MoCA actual costs and estimated Ethernet cabling
